limitations: Not randomised; dogs grouped by owner-chosen schools.

claims.statement: Dogs Trust recommends swapping items a dog should not have for something better ('fair trade') so the dog willingly releases items rather than guarding them.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Trade forbidden item for better reward.

claims.statement: To teach 'leave it', Dogs Trust advises waiting for the dog to look or move away from a low-value item, then marking and rewarding with a higher-value treat from the other hand.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Reinforce orientation away from forbidden item before adding cue.

claims.statement: Dogs Trust advises always returning to the dog before rewarding a stay, and rewarding while the dog is still in position—not as they get up.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Return before treat; avoid rewarding break from stay.

claims.statement: After a dog can stay ~10 seconds, Dogs Trust recommends unpredictable stay durations before reward so the dog cannot anticipate when to break the stay.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Vary seconds before reward after 10s baseline.
limitations: Ten-second benchmark is charity-specific, not universal research threshold.

claims.statement: Dogs Trust teaches that when the lead tightens, the handler stops walking and does not move forward until the lead is slack again.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Loose lead = forward motion; tight lead = stop.

claims.statement: Dogs Trust states that equipment promising to 'cure' pulling by causing pain or discomfort in sensitive areas is unnecessary and can be unpleasant and confusing for dogs; flat collar or comfortable harness is preferred.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Avoid pain/discomfort gear; use comfortable flat harness or collar.

claims.statement: Dogs Trust advises building time apart very gradually, pairing alone time with positive experiences such as long-lasting food toys, and reducing duration if stress signs appear.
claims.locator: Teach your dog how to be alone
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Gradual alone-time with positive association.
limitations: Prevention focus; not treatment for established separation anxiety.

claims.statement: Dogs Trust states that telling a dog off for separation-related destruction or toileting is likely to worsen anxiety because the dog does not understand the punishment in that context.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Punishment after absences can increase worry about owner return.
claims.confidenceJustification: Consistent with anxiety learning theory; charity guidance.

claims.statement: Dogs Trust advises avoiding leaving an adult dog alone for more than four hours, and building up more slowly if separation anxiety signs are present.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Four-hour general maximum; slower build if anxious.
claims.confidenceJustification: Common UK charity heuristic; individual dogs vary; not a statutory limit.
limitations: Not applicable uniformly to all ages or individual needs.

claims.statement: For dogs showing separation anxiety, Dogs Trust advises avoiding leaving them alone (or longer than they can cope) because continued absences can worsen the problem while longer-term support is arranged.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Avoid alone time beyond coping threshold during treatment.
claims.confidenceJustification: Standard clinical management advice from major UK charity.
limitations: Requires alternative care arrangements; app must signpost professional help.

claims.statement: Dogs Trust states the first step when behaviour concerns arise is to speak to a vet, who can examine the dog and refer to a behaviourist if needed.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Vet examination before behaviourist for behaviour change.

claims.statement: RSPCA advises never leaving a child alone in the same room as a dog, even the family dog.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Always supervise children and dogs together.
claims.confidenceJustification: Explicit safety rule repeated across UK charities.

claims.statement: RSPCA advises teaching children not to approach dogs when the dog is eating, sleeping, unwell, injured, tired, or near valued items.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Do not disturb dogs in vulnerable contexts.

claims.statement: Blue Cross advises not punishing dogs showing defensive behaviours such as growling, because punishment may suppress warnings and increase biting risk while adding stress.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Do not punish growling; seek behaviourist for aggression.

claims.statement: Blue Cross advises removing the dog from a worrying situation when stress signs appear (e.g. lip lick, growl, moving away) and giving a calming activity such as a chew or stuffed Kong.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Time out with positive focus when dog uncomfortable.

claims.statement: PDSA advises deducting food used in enrichment activities from the dog's daily ration to avoid weight gain.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Enrichment food comes from daily allowance.

claims.statement: PDSA states mental stimulation and enrichment should be balanced with adequate rest and downtime for dogs.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Enrichment balanced with sleep and rest.

claims.statement: ABTC's June 2024 indicative list includes electric/shock collars, choke chains/collars, and prong/pinch collars as aversive equipment that should not be used in training animals.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Lists shock, choke, prong among prohibited indicative equipment.

claims.statement: ABTC's indicative aversive methods list includes 'alpha roll'/pinning, hitting, hard lead jerks, and kneeing the dog as methods that should not be used.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Physical coercion methods listed as aversive.

claims.statement: Vieira de Castro et al. (2020) report dogs from schools using high proportions of aversive-based methods showed more stress-related behaviours and more tense/low behavioural states during training than dogs from reward-based schools (n=92 total across groups).
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Observational comparison of training schools; aversive-high group more stress behaviours.

claims.statement: Vieira de Castro et al. (2020) report dogs from highly aversive-based schools had higher post-training cortisol increases and more 'pessimistic' cognitive bias task performance than reward-trained dogs.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Cortisol and cognitive bias differences vs reward group.
limitations: Mixed-method schools partially overlapped on some measures.

protocols.title: Leave it — look away progression (Dogs Trust)
protocols.intendedOutcome: Dog orientates away from presented item on 'leave' cue without taking it.
inappropriateWhen: Resource guarding with aggression history without behaviourist plan

steps.instruction: Hold low-value item in one hand; when dog sniffs then looks or moves away, mark and reward from other hand with better treat.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Use more boring decoy item; higher-value reward.

steps.instruction: Add verbal cue 'leave' as item presented; mark and reward look-away.
steps.progressCriteria: Dog looks away on cue before item reachable.

steps.instruction: Generalise: new locations, item on floor, dropped from low height, gradually higher-value forbidden items.
steps.rewardTiming: Maintain high-value reward for difficult leaves.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Return to earlier step per Dogs Trust guidance.
failureModes: Progressing value or distraction too fast

reinforcementOptions: Fair trade swap if item already taken
welfareMonitoring: No escalation to snapping over items
stopConditions: Guarded resource with aggression—refer to behaviourist
safetyPrecautions: Use fair trade instead of force-taking items from mouth
referralRequirements: Persistent failure to leave—training classes or behaviourist

protocols.title: Loose-lead walking — stop-start method (Dogs Trust)
protocols.intendedOutcome: Dog walks with slack lead; forward motion contingent on loose lead.

steps.instruction: Reward dog for standing/sitting at handler side without lead; add lead when reliable.
When lead tightens, stop immediately; remain quiet until slack, then move forward.
steps.rewardTiming: Forward motion is reinforcer; optional treats at side.
steps.progressCriteria: Dog orients back and loosens lead to restart walk.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Walk opposite direction briefly to regain focus.

steps.instruction: Maintain consistency each walk; expect longer walks during learning phase.
steps.progressCriteria: Slack lead maintained with moderate distractions.

protocols.generalisationMaintenance: Consistent stop-start on every walk during learning.
safetyPrecautions: Do not use pain-based anti-pull devices per Dogs Trust and ABTC lists
protocols.appProgressionNotes: Dual-harness 'permission to pull' pattern noted as slower—optional advanced note only.

protocols.title: Alone-time preparation (puppy/adult prevention — Dogs Trust)
protocols.intendedOutcome: Dog remains relaxed during brief separations with positive alone-time associations.
inappropriateWhen: Established separation anxiety with panic—use management + professional support (see src-dt-separation-anxiety)
protocols.environment: Home; start with handler still in house.
protocols.baselineAssessment: Dog eats food toys calmly in handler presence.

steps.instruction: Use baby gate for brief visual separation; scatter treats or provide food toy before gate closes.
steps.rewardTiming: Calm behaviour reinforced with continued positive alone activity.
steps.progressCriteria: No stress signs (panting, pacing, vocalising) for brief period.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Stay closer to gate; shorten duration.

steps.instruction: Gradually increase time apart while owner in house, then very short departures with calm, low-key exits and returns.
steps.rewardTiming: Calm on return rewarded; no fuss on departure/arrival.
steps.progressCriteria: Short absences tolerated without stress signs.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Reduce seconds away; use dog sitter instead of stretching duration if anxiety present.

protocols.generalisationMaintenance: Routine alone practice below dog threshold.
welfareMonitoring: Stress signs listed by Dogs Trust—regress if seen
stopConditions: Any panic or injury risk—stop absences beyond threshold; contact behaviourist/vet
safetyPrecautions: Do not leave beyond four-hour charity heuristic if avoidable
referralRequirements: Separation anxiety signs → Dogs Trust Behaviour Support Line / vet / behaviourist
protocols.reviewReason: Separation-related; must not replace clinical behaviour modification plans.

behaviours.name: Leave item without taking
behaviours.observableCriteria: Dog withdraws nose/head from item within 2 seconds of 'leave' cue without contacting item.

behaviours.name: Walk with slack lead
behaviours.observableCriteria: Lead forms a relaxed U or J with no tension while handler walks at normal pace.

behaviours.name: Settle during brief separation
behaviours.observableCriteria: Dog consumes food toy or rests without pacing, excessive vocalising, or destruction for target duration.

lessons.title: Leave it — foundations
lessons.summary: Teach your dog to look away from tempting items and wait for a better reward.

lessons.title: Stop when the lead tightens
lessons.summary: Help your dog learn that a loose lead keeps the walk moving.

safetyRules.title: Always supervise children and dogs
safetyRules.rule: Never leave a child alone with a dog; teach do-not-disturb contexts and gentle interaction.

safetyRules.title: Do not punish warning signals
safetyRules.rule: Do not punish growling or other warnings; remove dog from trigger and seek vet/behaviourist support.
safetyRules.referralText: Veterinary assessment and accredited animal behaviourist.

safetyRules.title: Do not recommend ABTC-listed aversive tools or methods
safetyRules.rule: Good Dog must not recommend equipment or methods on ABTC indicative aversive lists (e.g. shock, choke, prong, alpha roll).

disagreements.question: Do low-proportion aversive methods in mixed training schools harm welfare outside training?
areasOfAgreement: Highly aversive school group showed worse stress, cortisol and cognitive bias than reward schools.
Mixed group showed more stress behaviours during training than reward group.
disagreements.disagreementSummary: Mixed and highly aversive groups did not differ on all measures (cognitive bias/cortisol in some comparisons); interpretation of 'low proportion' aversive use remains nuanced.
disagreements.goodDogPosition: Recommend reward-based training only; cite mixed-group stress behaviour finding without endorsing mixed methods.
researchGaps: Dose-response of aversive tools within otherwise reward-based plans

reviewItems.reason: Separation content must stay distinct from clinical separation anxiety treatment.
